currentDescription: In early 1989, Paul Cullen poured enough herbicide around the base of the Treaty Oak to kill 100 trees. He later claimed he was performing a magic ritual to protect a woman he loved. The tree, which had survived 500 years of floods and fires, began to die, prompting a massive rescue effort involving giant sunscreens and filtered water.

currentSubtitle: Forensic evidence of a dendrological murder
currentDescription: Samples from the tree were rushed to laboratories where the chemical Velpar was identified. The concentration was so high it was described as an "execution." Cullen was eventually arrested after boasting about the act in a local bookstore. He was sentenced to nine years in prison for criminal mischief.

currentSubtitle: Where the 1928 Master Plan was codified into law
currentDescription: The Austin City Council formally adopted the plan created by Koch & Fowler, which recommended the creation of a 'Negro District.' By concentrating all schools and services for Black residents in East Austin, the city found a way to enforce segregation without technically passing illegal racial zoning laws.

currentSubtitle: The physical line where the city cut off services
currentDescription: East Avenue (now I-35) became the hard border for the new district. Families who refused to move East found their water and electricity disconnected by the city. This forced migration was designed to empty thriving communities like Wheatville and Clarksville to make way for white development.

currentSubtitle: The closure of a community anchor
currentDescription: To force the migration, the city closed the Wheatville School, the primary educational center for Black families in West Austin. With no local school and no municipal services, the residents were left with no choice but to abandon their property and move to the designated district.

currentSubtitle: The site of the official refusal by Governor Colquitt
currentDescription: Governor Oscar Colquitt formally refused to host Washington, stating that a Black man should not be allowed to speak from the Capitol stand. The snub was intended to humiliate Washington, but it only served to mobilize the city's residents in protest.

currentSubtitle: 5,000 people gather at a former landfill to hear the truth
currentDescription: A crowd of over 5,000 people—nearly 20% of Austin's total population at the time—crammed into the square to hear Washington speak. The event was racially integrated, a rare occurrence in 1911, and the speech from the bandstand became a landmark moment in Austin's civil rights history.

currentSubtitle: Where the dam breached and eight workers died
currentDescription: On April 7, 1900, after days of torrential rain, a massive section of the granite dam gave way. The resulting wall of water obliterated the power house, killing eight workers instantly and destroying the city's municipal power and water systems. Chunks of granite the size of houses were carried miles downstream.

currentSubtitle: Massive chunks of the original dam still sit in the river
currentDescription: The ruins of the 1900 dam are still visible at Red Bud Isle. Massive, smooth granite blocks—remnants of the "world's greatest dam"—remain scattered in the water, serving as a permanent grave for the city's 19th-century industrial ambitions.

currentSubtitle: The scene of the $854.08 shortage
currentDescription: Porter worked as a teller at 6th and Congress. When federal bank examiners found a shortage in his accounts, he was accused of embezzlement. Porter panicked and fled to New Orleans, then Honduras, before the illness of his wife forced him to return to Austin to face trial.

currentSubtitle: Where William Sydney Porter became 'O. Henry'
currentDescription: Porter was held here after his arrest. While awaiting sentencing, he began writing short stories to support his daughter. He adopted the pen name 'O. Henry' to hide his criminal past from editors, a name that would soon become more famous than his own.

currentSubtitle: Where a pharmacist began sketching the world
currentDescription: When William Sydney Porter arrived in Austin in 1884, he was a 21-year-old pharmacist looking for a fresh start. He found it at Morley Brothers on East 8th Street. Between filling prescriptions, he was an obsessive observer, sketching the town's gamblers, cowboys, and elite who frequented the shop. The conversations he eavesdropped on here became the raw material for his early humorous writing.

currentSubtitle: Drafting the boundaries of a literary career
currentDescription: In 1887, Porter took a job as a draftsman at the Texas General Land Office, now the oldest state office building in Texas. He spent four years here mapping the wild geography of the state. The thick stone walls and bureaucratic atmosphere left a deep impression, later serving as the setting for his story "Bexar Scrip No. 2692." This was a period of stability where he married Athol Estes and began his humor magazine, The Rolling Stone.

currentSubtitle: The Hill City Quartette's favorite stage
currentDescription: Porter was a fixture at Scholz Garden, Austin's oldest biergarten and political hub. He was a gifted singer and a member of the Hill City Quartette, which performed German lieder and folk songs for the regulars. Scholz was more than a bar; it was where the town's German heritage and Texas politics collided. The museum still displays the chair and table he used, a physical link to the bohemian lifestyle he enjoyed before the embezzlement charges forced him into exile and prison.

currentSubtitle: 60 tons of tires, bathtubs, and a Buddha leaf
currentDescription: Vince Hannemann began building the cathedral in 1988. It features vaulted ceilings of bicycle wheels and a "throne" of electronics. The structure includes a leaf from the Buddha's tree of enlightenment encased in a specific chamber, making it a bizarre spiritual hub made of recycled waste.

currentSubtitle: The legal battle to save a mountain of trash
currentDescription: In 2010, the city nearly demolished the Cathedral after neighbor complaints. Hannemann mobilized engineers to prove the junk was structurally sound. After a high-stakes hearing and massive public support, the city issued a permit, officially legitimizing the junk as art.

currentSubtitle: The literal birthplace of PC's Limited
currentDescription: While a freshman, Michael Dell began upgrading computers and selling them directly to customers. The fire marshal eventually intervened when Dell had stacked so many cardboard boxes in the hallway that it became a fire hazard, forcing him to move his business off-campus.

currentSubtitle: The first "adult" office where the company nearly died
currentDescription: Following the Dobie Center eviction, Dell moved to this office. The growth was so explosive that the company struggled to manage inventory, nearly collapsing under its own weight before a pivot to custom-built machines saved the future empire.

currentSubtitle: Where Charles Whitman held the campus hostage
currentDescription: Whitman reached the 28th floor with a footlocker of rifles. From the 231-foot vantage point, he began picking off students and faculty below. The observation deck was eventually breached by Officers Ramiro Martinez and Houston McCoy, who ended the siege.

currentSubtitle: The "dead zone" where civilians fired back
currentDescription: The mall south of the tower was a killing field. Realizing the police were outgunned, local Austin citizens grabbed deer rifles from their trucks and began firing back at the tower. This improvised civilian response pinned Whitman down and prevented a higher death toll.

currentSubtitle: Where a teenage Stevie sat at the feet of Muddy Waters
currentDescription: Clifford Antone's original blues club on 6th Street was Vaughan's home. He spent his youth watching legends like Muddy Waters and Albert King, eventually developing the explosive, heavy-stringed style that would change rock history.

currentSubtitle: The permanent pilgrimage site for guitarists
currentDescription: The bronze statue at Auditorium Shores commemorates Vaughan's legacy. Fans from around the world leave flowers at his feet, and the statue is a central point for Austin music pilgrimages, standing near the site of many of his most famous performances.

currentSubtitle: 1.5 million residents who eat 20,000 lbs of bugs a night
currentDescription: The bridge's 18-inch-deep crevices are the perfect temperature for Mexican free-tailed bats. In the early 80s, residents called for their extermination until Dr. Merlin Tuttle of Bat Conservation International moved to Austin to save the colony, proving they were a massive benefit to the city.

currentSubtitle: An engineering fluke creates a bat sanctuary
currentDescription: When the Congress Avenue Bridge was reconstructed in 1980, engineers had no idea they were building a massive incubator. The 18-inch-deep expansion joints used in the design were accidentally the perfect temperature and width for Mexican free-tailed bats. By 1984, the population exploded to 750,000, and a city-wide panic ensued. Local newspapers ran sensationalist headlines about "rabid invaders," and petrified residents petitioned the city to exterminate the colony.

currentSubtitle: Dr. Merlin Tuttle turns fear into tourism
currentDescription: In 1986, bat expert Dr. Merlin Tuttle made a bold move: he relocated the headquarters of Bat Conservation International to Austin specifically to save the Congress Avenue colony. He launched a massive public education campaign, explaining that the bats eat 20,000 pounds of insects every single night. The panic turned into pride. Today, the colony has grown to 1.5 million bats, making it the largest urban colony in North America.

currentSubtitle: The 68-degree heart of Austin environmentalism
currentDescription: The natural springs were the catalyst for Austin's modern environmental laws. The springs are home to the endangered Barton Springs Salamander, which became the legal centerpiece of the fight to stop the Barton Creek PUD development.

currentSubtitle: The 15-hour "All-Night Public Hearing"
currentDescription: On June 7, 1990, a record-breaking crowd flooded the council chamber. Residents spoke until the sun rose, successfully pressuring the city to reject the massive development plan. This event remains the benchmark for political activism in Austin.

currentSubtitle: Where LBJ had his first date with Lady Bird
currentDescription: In 1934, LBJ met Claudia 'Lady Bird' Taylor for breakfast at the Driskill. He proposed shortly after. The hotel remained his political HQ throughout his career, including the night he watched the returns of his 1948 Senate race.

currentSubtitle: A beautification project that replaced trash with trails
currentDescription: In the 1970s, Lady Bird led a massive project to clean up the banks of Town Lake. Her influence replaced trash-strewn banks with thousands of flowering trees and the hike-and-bike trails that define downtown Austin today.

currentSubtitle: Jesse Driskill loses a $400,000 hotel in a poker game
currentDescription: Just two years after building the finest hotel in Texas, Jesse Driskill, an inveterate gambler, lost the entire building in a high-stakes poker game. He died bankrupt shortly after, and his spirit is said to haunt the halls to this day.

currentSubtitle: The site of the "Suicide Brides"
currentDescription: In Room 525, two separate brides committed suicide in the same bathtub, exactly 20 years apart to the day. The room was sealed for years before being reopened, and remains a central point for reported paranormal activity.

currentSubtitle: Where ten nuns and 90 children formed a human chain
currentDescription: As the storm surge breached the dormitory, the Sisters of Charity tied themselves to the children with clotheslines. They sang 'Queen of the Waves' to calm the orphans until the building collapsed. Only three boys survived by clinging to a salt cedar tree. The site is now occupied by a Walmart Supercenter.

currentSubtitle: The only sanctuary for the three boys who escaped
currentDescription: The salt cedar tree located on the orphanage grounds was the only thing that didn't wash away. Three orphans—Will Murney, Frank Madera, and Albert Campbell—clung to its branches through the night, witnessing the destruction of the asylum and the loss of their peers and the sisters.

currentSubtitle: The headquarters where "Death Star" strategies were born
currentDescription: Traders in the 50-story north tower coordinated artificial power outages in California while mocking "Grandma Millie" on recorded phone lines. The memos found here after the collapse described a sophisticated system of market manipulation that prioritized quarterly earnings over human safety.

currentSubtitle: Where a symbol of global power was sold to a waste management firm
currentDescription: Following Enron's bankruptcy filing, the iconic tilted "E" sign outside the headquarters was sold at auction for $44,000. It served as a visceral visual end to the company that once claimed to be "The World's Leading Company." The logo was eventually purchased by a local scrap and waste company.

currentSubtitle: The windowless room where the "Mail Slot" fix was designed
currentDescription: On April 13, 1970, the words "Houston, we've had a problem" echoed through this room. Engineers here worked for three days straight, building the prototype for the CO2 scrubber adapter using only a plastic bag, cardboard, and duct tape to match the items the astronauts had on board.

currentSubtitle: Where the power-up sequence was calculated
currentDescription: Because the Lunar Module was never meant to be a long-term lifeboat, engineers in this facility had to rewrite the spacecraft's entire operating manual in real-time. They calculated exactly how much battery power could be diverted to the heating systems without killing the crew's re-entry guidance.

currentSubtitle: A pier-based casino that outran the Texas Rangers
currentDescription: The Balinese Room was built on a 600-foot pier over the Gulf. Whenever the Texas Rangers raided, they had to walk the entire length of the pier. By the time they reached the casino floor, the staff had pushed buttons to flip gambling tables into ordinary buffets and hide the bands' instruments.

currentSubtitle: Where the "Free State" was managed by the mob
currentDescription: Sam and Rosario Maceo managed their empire from this location. Their influence was so absolute that the city's police chief and local government were openly on their payroll. The "Free State" provided a Depression-era economic boom that the rest of Texas lacked.

currentSubtitle: Where the SS Grandcamp detonated
currentDescription: On April 16, 1947, a fire broke out on the SS Grandcamp, carrying 2,300 tons of ammonium nitrate. A crowd gathered to watch the orange smoke, unaware that a massive detonation was imminent. The blast leveled the nearby Monsanto plant and killed over 500 people instantly.

currentSubtitle: Launched 1.6 miles by the force of the blast
currentDescription: This specific two-ton anchor was found embedded in the mud over a mile away from the explosion site. It stands today exactly where it landed, a visceral marker of the pressure wave that shattered windows 40 miles away in Houston.

currentSubtitle: Where rancher Robert Reed Ellison first recorded the orbs
currentDescription: Ellison reported the lights while driving a herd of cattle in 1883, initially fearing they were Apache signal fires. Today, the state-funded viewing area attracts thousands who witness the lights darting across the horizon in areas where no roads or power lines exist.

currentSubtitle: Where Clay Henry I held court and drank longnecks
currentDescription: The original Mayor, Clay Henry, was a local celebrity who won a mock election in 1986. He became a global news sensation for his ability to drink an entire bottle of beer in seconds. The trading post served as his "office" for years.

currentSubtitle: The memorial to a castrated political leader
currentDescription: In 2002, the mayor's successor, Clay Henry III, was at the center of a legal scandal when a man was arrested for "castrating the mayor" in a drunken rage. A bronze statue now stands in Lajitas to commemorate the animal mayors of the Big Bend.

currentSubtitle: The geyser that doubled the world's oil supply in a day
currentDescription: On January 10, 1901, the ground began to tremble as mud and gas erupted from the salt dome. A black geyser of oil shot twice as high as the derrick. Beaumont's population ballooned from 9,000 to 50,000 in months as the "Oil Age" was born.

currentSubtitle: The instant city built on black gold
currentDescription: Within weeks of the strike, Gladys City became the prototypical oil boomtown. It was a chaotic landscape of wooden derricks and tents where the price of water often exceeded the price of oil due to the massive influx of speculators.

currentSubtitle: Where 500 residents forced the Texas Rangers to wave the white flag
currentDescription: A mob of 500 local residents besieged a detachment of 20 Texas Rangers in an adobe house on the plaza. After four days, the Rangers surrendered their weapons—the only time in the organization's history they were forced to capitulate to a civilian mob.

currentSubtitle: The ancient deposits that sparked a border war
currentDescription: The ancient dry lakes north of the town had been used freely by the community for centuries. When white politicians attempted to claim the land and charge for salt, it triggered the racial and economic tension that exploded in San Elizario.

currentSubtitle: Where the border was physically relocated with concrete
currentDescription: In 1963, Presidents Kennedy and López Mateos agreed to end the dispute. Engineers dug a new, concrete-lined riverbed to ensure the border would never move again. Thousands of homes were demolished to make way for the new channel.

currentSubtitle: The "no man's land" that moved south
currentDescription: This location marks the original path of the Rio Grande before the flood of 1864. For a century, this tract of land was a source of constant tension between El Paso and Juárez, as residents lived on land that two nations claimed simultaneously.

currentSubtitle: The "shadow city" beneath Laredo's oldest square
currentDescription: During the Revolution, merchants and rebels used vaulted brick tunnels connecting basements to the Rio Grande. In recent years, construction crews and urban explorers have rediscovered sections of these contraband routes after sudden street collapses.

currentSubtitle: Where private cellars connected to the river bank
currentDescription: The historic buildings surrounding the plaza, including the structures that now form La Posada, were known hubs for secret activity. The tunnels were used to move silver bars and weapons between the U.S. and Mexico outside of customs.

currentSubtitle: Ten Cadillacs buried at the angle of Giza
currentDescription: Created by the art group Ant Farm in 1974, the installation was funded by Stanley Marsh 3. The cars are now covered in thousands of layers of spray paint as visitors are encouraged to leave their own mark on the tailfins.

currentSubtitle: Where the "Golden Age" of tailfins was conceived
currentDescription: Cadillac Ranch began as a radical vision by the San Francisco art collective Ant Farm. Members Chip Lord, Hudson Marquez, and Doug Michels wanted to create a monument to the American dream and the evolution of the tailfin. In 1974, they met with eccentric Amarillo billionaire Stanley Marsh 3 at his estate to pitch the idea. Marsh, known for his absurdist pranks, immediately funded the project. The installation was placed at the exact same angle as the Great Pyramid of Giza.

currentSubtitle: An ever-changing thick-skinned organism
currentDescription: In 1997, Cadillac Ranch was physically uprooted and moved two miles west to escape the encroaching urban sprawl of Amarillo. Stanley Marsh 3 famously encouraged visitors to spray-paint the cars, turning a static sculpture into a living, participatory artwork. Today, the cars are encased in thousands of layers of paint. Each visitor who adds a layer participates in a sanctioned act of vandalism that has made the site a global pilgrimage point on Route 66.

currentSubtitle: The dawn attack that ended the Red River War
currentDescription: Colonel Ranald Mackenzie's scouts discovered the winter camps of the Comanche, Kiowa, and Cheyenne. His troops descended the cliffs at dawn, forcing the tribes to flee and abandon their winter supplies and horse herds.

currentSubtitle: Where 1,400 horses were executed to starve the tribes
currentDescription: To ensure the tribes could not escape or hunt, Mackenzie ordered the slaughter of 1,400 captured horses. The stench of the massacre hung over the canyon for weeks. Without their mounts, the tribes were forced to walk 200 miles to the reservation.

currentSubtitle: Where Jesse Washington was dragged from the courtroom
currentDescription: On May 15, 1916, Jesse Washington was seized by a mob immediately after his conviction. He was dragged through the streets to the town square, where a massive crowd had gathered to participate in the torture and killing.

currentSubtitle: The site of the two-hour public atrocity
currentDescription: Washington was burned alive under a tree as thousands of residents watched. The postcards made from this event were used by the NAACP to expose the reality of lynching to the rest of the world, changing the legal trajectory of the U.S.

currentSubtitle: Standing inside a prehistoric earthquake
currentDescription: Inside the cave, visitors can look up to see the jagged ceiling that is the literal fault line separating the Hill Country from the coastal plains. The cave was formed by tectonic shifts rather than water erosion, making it a unique geological window.

currentSubtitle: Where starving settlers dug mud huts into the ground
currentDescription: After being abandoned by their noble sponsors, settlers arrived in New Braunfels with no lumber or shelter. They dug "Erdhütten" (earth-huts) into the hillside to survive a winter of cholera and starvation, eventually founding the most distinct German corridor in Texas.

currentSubtitle: Prince Carl chooses a sanctuary in the wilderness
currentDescription: In March 1845, Prince Carl of Solms-Braunfels led 200 exhausted German immigrants to the junction of the Comal and Guadalupe Rivers. They had survived a nightmare journey from the coast where hundreds of their kin had died of cholera. Prince Carl, captivated by the crystalline waters of the Comal springs, purchased the land and named the settlement after his family seat in Germany. It was the birth of the state's most culturally distinct corridor.

currentSubtitle: The oldest dance hall in the Lone Star State
currentDescription: Built in 1878 by Henry Gruene, this 6,000-square-foot tin-roofed building is the oldest continually operating dance hall in Texas. It survived the Great Depression, the collapse of the cotton market, and the modernization of rural music. In the 1970s, the hall became a pilgrimage site for the emerging outlaw country scene. George Strait, Willie Nelson, and Lyle Lovett all honed their craft on its creaky wooden stage.

currentSubtitle: Roosevelt's recruitment center for the Spanish-American War
currentDescription: Roosevelt used the bar to find cowboys, Texas Rangers, and Ivy League athletes for the 1st U.S. Volunteer Cavalry. The bar is a meticulous replica of the House of Lords pub in London and remains a central point for Roosevelt-related ghost sightings.

currentSubtitle: The finest hotel west of the Mississippi
currentDescription: In 1859, German immigrant William Menger realized his dream by building a luxurious hotel right next to the ruins of the Alamo. It was an immediate sensation, featuring the first enclosed swimming pool in Texas and the finest cellar in the region. Every U.S. president from Ulysses S. Grant to George H.W. Bush has stayed here. The hotel's limestone walls have witnessed the entire transformation of Texas from a wild frontier into an industrial powerhouse.

currentSubtitle: A chambermaid who never left the third floor
currentDescription: On March 28, 1876, a 26-year-old chambermaid named Sallie White was shot in the street by her common-law husband after an argument. She died in the hotel two days later. The hotel management was so devastated they paid for her entire funeral. Today, Sallie is the Menger's most frequently reported apparition. Guests in the third-floor hallway often see a woman in a long Victorian skirt and a white apron carrying fresh towels; she vanishes as soon as she is approached.

currentSubtitle: Where San Antonio's "Chili Capital" reputation was built
currentDescription: The Chile Queens set up charcoal fires every night, serving spicy stews to everyone from soldiers to city elites. Their open-air festivals were a primary tourist draw until the city modernization led to their forced closure in the 1930s.

currentSubtitle: The historic night-market for San Antonio's street food
currentDescription: Before moving to Milam Park and Market Square, the Queens dominated Military Plaza. This was the original location where the "chili con carne" was standardized and exported to the rest of the world through the tourists who ate there.

currentSubtitle: Where 110-degree heat turned a spark into an inferno
currentDescription: On July 8, 1860, a fire destroyed most of the Dallas business district. Hysteria gripped the town as leaders claimed it was a slave uprising. This "Texas Troubles" panic led to vigilante groups patrolling the state looking for abolitionist spies.

currentSubtitle: The execution of Patrick, Samuel, and Cato
currentDescription: Without evidence, three enslaved men were seized and taken to the riverbank. They were lynched by a mob as the town sought scapegoats for the disaster. The event pushed Texas further toward secession and the Civil War.

currentSubtitle: Where Clyde lies next to his brother, Marvin
currentDescription: Following the 1934 ambush, Bonnie's mother refused to allow a joint burial, famously stating, "He had her in life, but he can't have her in death." Clyde was buried here in a remote, often overgrown cemetery that remains a site for "outlaw tourism."

currentSubtitle: The tiny town where a legend began
currentDescription: Willie Taliaferro Nelson was born April 29, 1933, in this tiny cotton town. Raised by his grandparents, he took music lessons from mail-order catalogs and wrote his first song at age seven. The town of Abbott (population 356) remains a pilgrimage site for fans, where the small Methodist church he once attended is still standing.

currentSubtitle: Rescuing Trigger from the flames
currentDescription: By 1970, Willie was a successful Nashville songwriter ("Crazy", "Hello Walls") but a failure as a recording artist. In a dramatic turning point, his Nashville home caught fire. Willie famously ran into the burning building to save two things: his guitar "Trigger" and a pound of marijuana. He took the disaster as a sign that his time in Nashville was over.

currentSubtitle: Chaos and country music in the rain
currentDescription: In 1973, Willie threw his first 4th of July Picnic at Dripping Springs. The lineup was a Texas dream: Waylon Jennings, Kris Kristofferson, and Doug Sahm. However, the event descended into beautiful chaos when torrential rains hit. Despite the mayhem, the Picnic became a foundational myth for the Austin music scene, an annual rite of passage that has continued for over 50 years.

currentSubtitle: A movie set turned into a private sanctuary
currentDescription: Located in Spicewood, "Luck" is Willie Nelson's private ranch, named after the 1880s Western movie set built for the film "Red Headed Stranger." Willie famously says: "When you're here, you're in Luck. When you leave, you're out of Luck." The site includes a chapel, a general store, and an opera house where he hosts exclusive concerts.

currentSubtitle: A homecoming sanctuary for Black veterans
currentDescription: Johnny Holmes opened the Victory Grill on August 15, 1945—the day Japan surrendered—as a place for returning Black soldiers to feel at home in a segregated city. It quickly evolved from a restaurant into a premier blues and jazz venue. Every major African American act touring the South played here, including Bobby Bland, Gatemouth Brown, and Janis Joplin. In 1988, a devastating fire nearly destroyed the building, but it was painstakingly restored as a National Historic Landmark.

currentSubtitle: Named for a hero, built for the community
currentDescription: Named after the Pearl Harbor hero Doris Miller, this East Austin auditorium was a massive pillar of the Chitlin' Circuit. During segregation, it was one of the few large-scale venues in Texas where Black artists like Ella Fitzgerald and Ike & Tina Turner could perform for Black audiences without harassment. Its sheer scale allowed the community to congregate in a way that smaller clubs could not.

currentSubtitle: The integration of the East 11th corridor
currentDescription: In the 1950s and 60s, Charlie's Playhouse was the hottest ticket in Austin. While most of the city was strictly segregated, Charlie's became a "cross-over" club where adventurous white students from UT would cross East Avenue to hear authentic R&B and blues. The venue was part of a thriving entertainment district that included dozens of Black-owned businesses, a world that was largely destroyed when the city used "urban renewal" funds to bulldoze much of the corridor in the 1970s.

currentSubtitle: Sawdust and southern fried cooking on South Lamar
currentDescription: James White opened the Broken Spoke in 1964 when South Lamar was just a dusty road on the outskirts of town. He built the original tin structure himself, serving chicken-fried steak and hosting legendary acts like Bob Wills and Tex Ritter. The original sawdust floor and low ceilings have remained unchanged for six decades.

currentSubtitle: The King of Country plays for $500 a night
currentDescription: In the late 1970s, a young and unknown George Strait played the Broken Spoke regularly with his Ace in the Hole Band. Long before he was selling out stadiums, he was playing for a few hundred dollars and a pitcher of beer. The walls of the Spoke are now a museum of country music history, covered in photos of Strait, Dolly Parton, and Kris Kristofferson.

currentSubtitle: "I'd rather be broke and keep the Spoke"
currentDescription: By the early 2000s, the land under the Broken Spoke was worth tens of millions of dollars. Developers built five-story luxury apartment complexes that now tower over the small tin building, literally surrounding it on all sides. James White famously refused every buyout offer. After his death in 2021, his family continued to run the hall, maintaining the tradition of live country music every night.

currentSubtitle: Vaudeville and twinkling stars on Congress Avenue
currentDescription: Opened in 1915 as "The Majestic," this vaudeville house was designed by John Eberson to be an "atmospheric" experience. The ceiling was painted to look like a night sky with twinkling electric stars, a wonder for early 20th-century Austin. The theater hosted every major traveling act of the era, including a legendary performance by Houdini.

currentSubtitle: Saving a landmark from the wrecking ball
currentDescription: By the 1970s, the theater had fallen into serious disrepair. It was part of a franchise showing kung fu and blaxploitation films, and the building was slated for demolition as part of a downtown redevelopment plan. A grassroots campaign led by the Austin Heritage Society saved the theater in 1975, renaming it The Paramount. This restoration was the first major win for the city's modern preservation movement.

currentSubtitle: The premiere venue for the film capital of the South
currentDescription: In the 1990s, director Richard Linklater's Austin Film Society made the Paramount its primary home for classic and independent screenings. The theater's status was further cemented as the main stage for SXSW Film premieres. Today, the Paramount hosts over 200 events annually, from the Austin Film Festival to national comedy acts, standing as the most active and successful historic preservation project in the state of Texas.

currentSubtitle: A German immigrant's sanctuary in the capital
currentDescription: In 1866, German immigrant and former Confederate soldier August Scholz opened a boarding house and beer garden on San Jacinto Boulevard. It immediately became the social hub for the city's thriving German population. In 1879, it became the home of the Austin Saengerrunde, a German singing society that still owns the building today. The garden survived Prohibition by selling "near beer" and bratwurst.

currentSubtitle: Pitchers of beer and the levers of power
currentDescription: Located just three blocks from the Texas Capitol, Scholz Garden became the unofficial clubhouse for the state legislature. LBJ and Ann Richards were regulars, and generations of lobbyists and lawmakers have settled political scores at its long wooden tables. Every election night, the garden is the site of massive watch parties where the state's political future is debated in real-time.

currentSubtitle: The ultimate pre-game ritual for over 100 years
currentDescription: For as long as UT has played football, Longhorn fans have gathered at Scholz Garden before and after games. The biergarten atmosphere, complete with a vintage bowling alley and oom-pah bands, creates a unique Texas-German fusion found nowhere else. The Saengerrunde's refusal to sell ensured its survival. Today, it remains a living time capsule where a freshman and a state senator can share a pitcher of Shiner.

currentSubtitle: The Father of Texas returns to the capital
currentDescription: The cemetery was established in 1851 specifically to provide a final resting place for Stephen F. Austin. He had died penniless in a small cabin in 1836, and his body was moved here from a remote plantation. His massive monument at the center of the grounds established the site as the state's primary secular shrine.

currentSubtitle: A voice for the Constitution in the heart of Texas
currentDescription: Barbara Jordan, the first Southern Black woman in Congress, is buried here, making her one of the most prominent African American figures in the cemetery. Her grave stands in a section that once only honored the state's white elite, a powerful symbol of the progress of civil rights in Texas.

currentSubtitle: Transforming a neglected yard into a national monument
currentDescription: By the early 1990s, the cemetery had fallen into serious disrepair, with toppled stones and overgrown weeds. Governor George W. Bush championed a $4.8 million restoration that added a state-of-the-art visitors center and extensive new landscaping. The project transformed the site into an active memorial and a major tourist attraction.

currentSubtitle: 775 feet above the Colorado River
currentDescription: Mt. Bonnell is the highest point within Austin city limits, a sheer limestone cliff offering a 360-degree view of Lake Austin and the downtown skyline. Named after George W. Bonnell, a Commissioner of Indian Affairs who allegedly leaped to his death from the cliff in 1842 to avoid capture by a Comanche raiding party, the site is steeped in local lore.

currentSubtitle: Steamboats and dances at the Lover's Leap
currentDescription: Since the 1850s, Mt. Bonnell has been the city's primary social destination. In the mid-19th century, visitors would take steamboats up the Colorado River to the base of the mountain and hike to the top for picnics and dances. A popular superstition developed: if a couple climbs the mountain together, they will fall in love.

currentSubtitle: Wildflowers and the protection of the river corridor
currentDescription: Lady Bird Johnson considered the view from Mt. Bonnell to be her favorite in all of Austin. She used her national influence to advocate for the preservation of the natural beauty of the river corridor that stretches below the summit. The wildflowers that carpet the slopes each spring are a direct result of her highway beautification efforts.

currentSubtitle: The Emporium and the breakout of Wooderson
currentDescription: This drive-in burger joint served as "The Emporium," the central hangout where the film's characters congregate. It was here that Matthew McConaughey improvised the line "alright, alright, alright," which became a global catchphrase. Top Notch is still open and almost entirely unchanged since its 1971 opening.

currentSubtitle: Party at the tower under the artificial moon
currentDescription: The film's climactic keg party was filmed at a real Austin moonlight tower near Hemphill Park. These 165-foot towers, originally installed in 1894 to catch a serial killer, are unique to Austin—the only surviving system in the world. Linklater used the tower as a symbol of the city's weird and enduring heritage.

currentSubtitle: The hazing rituals of Huntsville and Austin
currentDescription: The school scenes, including the iconic first-day-of-school hazing rituals, were filmed at Bedichek Middle School during the summer break. Linklater, who grew up in Huntsville, Texas, set the film in Austin because he considered it the "freest place in Texas." The success of the film helped establish the infrastructure for the Austin film industry.

currentSubtitle: The Burroughs plantation and the walk to Malden
currentDescription: Washington was born enslaved on April 5, 1856, on a small tobacco plantation in Virginia. He never knew his father, a white man from a neighboring farm. At age nine, following emancipation, he walked with his family to West Virginia to work in salt furnaces and coal mines. This period of extreme labor shaped his later philosophy that economic independence through manual work was the only path to Black advancement.

currentSubtitle: An entrance exam involving a broom and a duster
currentDescription: At age 16, Washington walked 500 miles to reach the Hampton Institute. His entrance exam was an unconventional test of character: a teacher told him to clean a recitation room. Washington swept the floor three times and dusted every surface four times. When the teacher returned and could find no dirt, she quietly said, "I guess you will do to enter this institution."

currentSubtitle: A school built from the clay of a cotton field
currentDescription: In 1881, Washington arrived in Tuskegee, Alabama, to find a school that existed only on paper. With no land and only a small state appropriation, he borrowed money to buy an abandoned plantation. His students literally built the school from the ground up—clearing the land, making their own bricks, and constructing the first buildings. By the time of his death, Tuskegee had over 1,500 students and 100 buildings.

currentSubtitle: The speech that split a movement
currentDescription: On September 18, 1895, Washington delivered his most famous and controversial speech at the Cotton States Exposition. He told a mostly white audience: "Cast down your bucket where you are," arguing that Black Americans should accept social segregation in exchange for economic opportunity. The speech made him a national hero to whites and the most powerful Black man in America, but it also earned him the lifelong opposition of W.E.B. Du Bois.

currentSubtitle: A historic meal that triggered a national scandal
currentDescription: On October 16, 1901, President Theodore Roosevelt invited Washington to dinner at the White House—the first time a Black American had dined there as a guest. The backlash from the white South was volcanic; newspapers described the dinner as a "national outrage." Roosevelt, stunned by the intensity of the racism, never invited another Black guest to a formal dinner.

currentSubtitle: Raised in a drugstore in Greensboro
currentDescription: Porter was born September 11, 1862, in Greensboro, NC. His mother died when he was only three, and he was raised by his aunt in a house filled with books and sketching paper. At age 15, he began an apprenticeship at his uncle's drugstore, eventually becoming a licensed pharmacist. The regulars at the shop became the prototypes for his later characters.

currentSubtitle: Fleeing the law in a country with no treaty
currentDescription: When federal auditors indicted Porter for a $5,654.20 shortage at the First National Bank in 1896, he made a snap decision that ruined his reputation: he fled. He took a train to New Orleans and then a steamer to Honduras, one of the few countries without a US extradition treaty. He spent six months living as a bohemian, reportedly befriending the infamous bank robber Al Jennings.

currentSubtitle: A master writer is born in a prison cell
currentDescription: Convicted in February 1898, Porter served three years in the Ohio State Penitentiary in Columbus. His training as a pharmacist saved him from hard labor; he was assigned to the prison hospital. In the quiet of the night shifts, he began writing short stories to support his daughter, adopting the pen name "O. Henry" to protect his identity. He published 14 stories from prison.

currentSubtitle: The master of the twist ending dies in the dark
currentDescription: After prison, Porter moved to New York City in 1902 and entered a period of staggering productivity, writing a story a week for the New York World. He became a celebrity, known for his reclusive habits. He died at age 47 in a New York hotel room from cirrhosis. His last words were a final touch of O. Henry irony: "Turn up the lights. I don't want to go home in the dark."
